messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At seventy-four, Samir was conducting a routine chemical containment sweep at the Cedar Ridge remediation site when the calibration error he had signed off on proved catastrophic. A corroded valve ruptured under pressure, releasing a plume of industrial solvent that flared onto his junior technician’s arms and face. Samir remembered the sudden hiss of escaping gas, the frantic scramble for the emergency shower, and the sickening realization that his oversight had permanently scarred a colleague’s body. The incident report was sealed, but in Samir’s mind, the event never settled. He began to view the world through a lens of quiet vulnerability, convinced that structural failure was always waiting beneath the surface of everyday routines. Over the following months, the memory of the accident refused to integrate into a coherent timeline. Samir knew precisely what had transpired, yet when he attempted to recount it to his wife or former colleagues, the words simply vanished. The experience lodged behind his ribs, untranslatable, which only deepened his isolation. When the house grew quiet, the memory would intrude with violent immediacy. He would be reviewing historical water tables at his drafting table, and suddenly the air would seem to thicken with the phantom acridness of the chemical flare. His hands would freeze over the blueprints, and for a terrifying stretch, he was certain he was back in the rupture, living the catastrophe in real time. The sheer extremity of these flashbacks made him question his own grip on reality; he found himself reading the official incident report repeatedly, searching for a version of events that felt more plausible, because the alternative was too harrowing to accept as fact. This unwordable intrusion was directly activated by the sensory landscape of his daily work. At the county environmental monitoring station where Samir spent his mornings logging soil samples, heavy breathing sounds acted as a direct conduit back to the untranslatable terror. The moment those ragged breaths cut through the climate-controlled air, his focus collapsed. The auditory cue pulled him immediately into the reliving phase, where the past and present bled together until he could no longer distinguish the monitoring station from the ruptured valve. This cycle tightened with repetition, leaving him exhausted by the time his shift ended. He had come to interpret ease itself as a danger. When the afternoon sun warmed his shoulders or a successful audit left him feeling unburdened, that fleeting sense of happiness would act as a direct cue, pulling him forward into the same inescapable recollection. Similarly, when his wife reached for him in the evening, attempting a familiar hug to ground him, the physical affection felt suffocating. The press of her arms against his chest mirrored the loss of control he had felt at the site, and the touch alone would drag the unwordable memory back into his awareness, forcing him back into the reliving phase before he could steady himself. The cumulative effect of this narrowing was profound. Once a man who had spent decades mapping ecological recovery, Samir now found himself confined to the periphery of his field. He stopped attending departmental briefings, telling himself he was simply focusing on archival work, though in truth he lacked the capacity to endure the unpredictability of shared spaces. The avoidance patterns had calcified into a quiet routine. He woke early, worked alone in his study, and carefully regulated his breathing to stay beneath the threshold of recall. At seventy-eight, the weight of the past had finally become too heavy to carry alone. He sought therapy not because he wanted to relive the site accident, but because the inescapable memories and the triggering sensory landscape had eroded his ability to function in the present. He was terrified that his wife would eventually tire of his distance, and yet he clung to the faint hope that someone might help him untangle the knot between his guilt and his survival, so he could finally rest without the constant threat of the past returning.
